extracted.intended_audience: DEA registrants, licensees, administrative law practitioners, and attorneys handling controlled-substances registrations
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing DEA revocation of a practitioner's controlled-substances registration when the practitioner lacks state authority (e.g., due to suspension of a state medical license). Includes statutory bases, regulatory default rules, service/mailing proof, official-notice practice, and post-order procedural steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: State licensure as a prerequisite for DEA registration
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must be authorized to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the State in which the practitioner practices in order to obtain and maintain a DEA registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites statutory direction that the Attorney General shall register practitioners only if the applicant is authorized to dispense controlled substances under state law (21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)) and the CSA definition of 'practitioner' requiring state authorization (21 U.S.C. 802(21)). The Agency treats possession of state authority to dispense as a fundamental condition for registration and will revoke registration where the registrant is not authorized by state law to dispense controlled substances (discussion and supporting cases, e.g., Gonzales v. Oregon, and prior DEA decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for revocation under 21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Attorney General is authorized to suspend or revoke a registration upon finding the registrant has had his State license suspended or revoked and is no longer authorized by State law to engage in dispensing of controlled substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct statutory citation: 21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3). The Decision applies this provision to revoke the registrant's DEA certificate because the registrant's Florida osteopathic license was suspended, rendering him ineligible to maintain DEA registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'practitioner' under the CSA
rubrics_metrics.description: The CSA defines 'practitioner' to include physicians 'licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by the United States or the jurisdiction in which he practices' to dispense controlled substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 21 U.S.C. 802(21) and explains that this statutory definition ties federal registration eligibility to state licensing status, supporting revocation when state authority is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of default and failure to request a hearing (21 CFR 1301.43)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a registrant fails to file a written request for hearing in response to an Order to Show Cause, the registrant is deemed to have waived the right to a hearing and be in default; a default constitutes admission of the factual allegations of the OSC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory citations: 21 CFR 1301.43 (including 1301.43(e) and (f)(1)). Where default occurs, DEA may file a Request for Final Agency Action (RFAA) and the Administrator may enter a default final order pursuant to 21 CFR 1316.67. The Decision treats the OSC allegations as admitted due to the registrant's default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of service and proof of service standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Service attempts and mailing evidence (e.g., attempted personal service, certified mail delivery with tracking showing 'left with individual') can establish adequate service of the OSC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Government's submission of investigator declarations showing attempted personal service and later certified-mail delivery with tracking was relied upon to find service adequate (see RFAAX 2). The Decision describes reliance on those factual service records in finding proper notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency official notice and the right to show contrary evidence (5 U.S.C. 556(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may take official notice of facts at any stage; however, if a decision rests on official notice of a material fact not in the record, the party is entitled, on timely request, to an opportunity to show the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 5 U.S.C. 556(e) and the Attorney General's Manual on the APA. In this Decision, the Agency took official notice of Florida online licensing records and informed the registrant he may dispute the finding by filing a properly supported motion for reconsideration within 15 calendar days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion for reconsideration: timing and filing procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A registrant may file a properly supported motion for reconsideration of findings of fact within fifteen calendar days of the date of the Order; motions and responses must be filed and served by email to specified DEA addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Decision specifies the 15-calendar-day deadline and directs filings and service by email to the other party and to the Office of the Administrator, Drug Enforcement Administration, at dea.addo.attorneys@dea.gov. Motions should be properly supported to dispute any official-noticed material facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: State statutory definitions relevant to dispensing and practitioner status (Florida statutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Florida law defines when a practitioner may prescribe/dispense controlled substances, defines 'dispense' as transfer of possession to ultimate consumer (or intermediary for ultimate consumer), and includes osteopathic physicians in the 'practitioner' definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Fla. Stat. § 893.05(1)(a) (practitioner may prescribe/dispense in good faith and in course of professional practice), Fla. Stat. § 893.02(7) (definition of 'dispense'), Fla. Stat. § 893.02(23) (definition of 'practitioner'), and chapter 459 (definition of osteopathic physician). The Decision uses these definitions to determine that a suspended osteopathic license removes state authorization to dispense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior agency decisions and judicial precedent to support revocation
rubrics_metrics.description: DEA relies on its prior administrative decisions and relevant judicial opinions to apply the rule that state disqualification from practice warrants revocation of DEA registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Decision cites cases and previous DEA final orders (e.g., James L. Hooper, M.D.; Frederick Marsh Blanton, M.D.; Sheran Arden Yeates, M.D.; and Gonzales v. Oregon) as precedent demonstrating consistent application of the principle that loss of state authority to dispense justifies revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to revoke registration, deny renewal/modification, and set effective date
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrator's authority to revoke the DEA certificate and to deny pending applications for renewal, modification, or additional registration in the State where the registrant lacks state authority; the Order states an effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order invokes 28 CFR 0.100(b) and statutory authority (21 U.S.C. 824(a); 21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)) to revoke Certificate of Registration No. FP0455142, deny pending applications, and sets the Order effective date (here, September 19, 2025). The signing/filing procedures and administrative signature practices are described (DEA Federal Register Liaison Officer filing for publication without altering legal effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings of fact from undisputed record evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When factual allegations are admitted (by default) or supported by undisputed official records, the Agency will find those facts and base the legal disposition on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Decision finds that the registrant's Florida osteopathic license remains suspended based on Florida online records (which the Agency took official notice of) and that, because the registrant lacks authority to practice, he is not authorized to dispense controlled substances in Florida; accordingly, revocation follows.
